newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/mark sags in Europe, Tietmeyer deals mild blow.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark sags in Europe, Tietmeyer deals mild blow.

text.p: The dollar suffered a setback against the mark in Europe's afternoon as Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer quashed sentiment by saying the bank was not interested in seeing the mark weaken further.
His remark sparked a flurry of mark buying against the dollar and the yen, though the shock was softened by Tietmeyer's comment that the mark's current level reflected fundamentals.

"It's the first time in a long while that they've (German authorities) come out and said something about currency levels," said one trader at a British bank. "The Japanese have been the ones who were more obviously worried about currency levels."
The impact of the comment was seen as temporary, however.
"People are going to try and pick up dollars again soon, as the dollar uptrend is still in place," the trader said.
The dollar edged back up slightly later on, and was at 1.7255/60 marks at 1520 GMT against 1.7281/86 in late European trade on Wednesday.
Analysts said Tietmeyer's remark was aimed not at pushing dollar/mark lower but at slowing down the speed of its rise.
"It's consistent with the view that Germany is quite happy with the mark on the soft side but not falling rapidly," said Ian Gunner, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank here.

"I think it's the pace (of dollar/mark) more than anything else... By saying the mark reflects fundamentals he's saying the mark's weakness is justified by what's happening to the economy," Gunner said.
Tietmeyer's comments momentarily eclipsed the U.S. trade figures, which were announced just before the Bundesbank chief's news conference and which had until then held the market's attention.
The U.S. February trade deficit shrank to $11.59 billion from January's $12.67 billion, but was still above forecasts of $10.1 billion.
However, the keenly watched trade deficit with Japan shrank slightly to $4.26 billion from January's $4.29 billion.

"The dollar responded very well to the data, and the US-Japan aspect of the data was very encouraging as we'd expected a widening (in the trade gap), so there was a lot of relief over that," said Don Smith, international economist at HSBC Markets.
The dollar was at 125.95/05 yen at 1550 GMT, off the day's high but up from 125.62/72 in late Europe on Wednesday.
Buying of marks for yen following Tietmeyer's comment on the mark also helped dollar/yen, but the trade figures had been the key, traders said.
The market had been awaiting the trade data with some trepidation, particularly after a remark from U.S. Deputy Trade Secretary Lawrence Summers warning about the US-Japan trade gap.

Summers said overnight that Japan needed economic expansion based on domestic demand in order to avoid the kind of strains seen in the past -- an apparent reference to the friction between the two trading partners.
In addition, Japan had also announced its trade data overnight, revealing that its trade surplus with the U.S. in March grew by 11 percent from the previous year to 379.8 billion yen.

There was little reaction to comments by Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin which were seen as in line with recent remarks from the Fed. Rivlin said the U.S. economy was strong and its labour markets very tight, but also said inflation was well-behaved.
Meanwhile, the mark was mostly steady against other European currencies. The British pound dipped against the mark on Tietmeyer's comment but cable was range-bound.

The Canadian dollar weakened to a 23-month low against the U.S. dollar amid talk of central bank intervention to support it. It was at 1.3965 per U.S. dollar against 1.3972 late on Wednesday.--Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex Desk, +44-171-542-6721
